name: Perilla seed extract

lead: Perilla seed extract comes from Perilla frutescens, a mint-family herb used in Korean, Chinese, Japanese and Indian cooking; the seeds are roughly 38 to 45 percent oil. It appears in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, used for softer, smoother, more comfortable skin.

The chain is barrier support: the plant oils soften the skin surface, and the extract and its component luteolin reduced inflammatory signalling in animal and cell studies. Published work is limited to laboratory and animal studies; human appearance trials were not found.

paras: Used in creams, oils and serums as a botanical emollient step after cleansing, often layered with other moisturising ingredients. Users typically describe softer skin soon after application and a gradual improvement in comfort and smoothness over weeks.
Perilla seed allergy, including anaphylaxis, is documented in children and adults, and contact dermatitis can occur from handling. People with seed allergies commonly avoid it.

angle.text: Perilla seed extract is included in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, used for softer, smoother skin. The oil-rich seed softens the skin surface, and the extract reduced inflammatory signalling in animal and cell studies.

lead: Perilla seed extract is derived from the seeds of Perilla frutescens, a mint-family annual used in Korean, Chinese, Japanese and Indian cooking; the seeds contain roughly 38 to 45 percent oil.[1] It appears in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 or antioxidant ingredient.

Published work consists mainly of laboratory and animal studies, including anti-inflammatory effects in mouse colitis models and an in vitro hair-loss study.[2][3][4] Perilla seed allergy is documented in children, and handling can cause contact dermatitis.[1][5] No clinical study of perilla seed extract for skin appearance was found.

paras: Perilla seeds and their oil are culinary ingredients in Korea, where toasted seed powder and oil season dishes, and the plant is also used in traditional medicine in parts of Southeast Asia.[1]

A 2025 mouse study reported that perilla seed extract and its component luteolin reduced inflammation in an inflammatory bowel disease model, and a 2024 study reported similar findings in ulcerative colitis models.[2][6] A 2025 in vitro study examined supercritical-fluid extracts for anti-hair-loss potential.[4] These are not human appearance trials.

Eating large quantities of seeds has caused anaphylaxis, and handling leaves or oil may cause contact dermatitis.[1] A study of 21 children characterised clinical and immunological features of perilla seed allergy and noted the lack of a diagnostic test.[5]
No studies found on perilla seed extract for skin or appearance. Human data are limited to allergy case series.[5]
